summary:
Elazığ province stands under the national framework of Turkey, where homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, and where discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in law. The same framework withholds recognition of same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption, and bars LGBTI people from serving openly in the military. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia.

Legislative risk is live rather than hypothetical. A leaked omnibus draft law dated 29 October 2025, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" with penalties of up to three years, would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by imposing a minimum age of 25 and onerous eligibility conditions, and would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The package also carries unrelated measures, including longer sentences for child offences and online-content removal. Whether it has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Hostility is not confined to statute. On 19 December 2022 an anti-LGBT hate rally was held at Elazığ's Cumhuriyet (Republic) Square under a banner reading "LGBT sapkınlıktır" ("LGBT is perversion"), with the participation of ruling AKP deputy mayor Nazif Bilginoğlu. The rally statement denounced consensual same-sex relationships and "homosexual marriage" as a "revolting loss of reason" in Western states, deployed the terms "perverse" and "degenerate mentality", and tied gender and sexual themes to Turkey's denunciation of the Istanbul Convention. The event records state-facilitated, locally active anti-LGBT mobilisation in this province, which bears directly on what a visibly LGBTQ traveller can expect on the ground.

Since 2015 the Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned and forcibly dispersed Pride marches, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In early 2026 the government was considering criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality", extending the same framing beyond private conduct to speech.
tangentialFactors:
Turkey's position in regional comparisons is near the floor of the ranking: 47th of 49 in the 2026 Rainbow Europe index, above only Azerbaijan and Russia, which gives a visitor a rough sense of how far the country sits from regional norms of protection.

The draft package's justification — protecting "the family" and "public morals" — is the same framing the Erdoğan government has used to legitimise stigmatisation, and the Elazığ rally statement's attacks on Western recognition of same-sex relationships and its linkage to the Istanbul Convention denunciation show that framing operating at municipal level, not only in Ankara.

The 11th Judicial Package does not stand alone: it carries longer child sentences and online-content removal alongside the anti-LGBT provisions, indicating a broader penal and social-conservatism agenda rather than a measure aimed solely at LGBT people.

The criminalisation threat targets the supply side of transition as well as trans people themselves — the professionals providing gender-affirming care face charges — so continuity of medication and treatment during a stay is exposed to the same legislative risk as the visitor's own conduct.
localsOnly:
Residents of Elazığ live under a legal position in which homosexuality has not been a crime since 1858 and gender-reassignment surgery has been lawful since 1988, and in which the constitution and statutes prohibit discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, while the state offers no recognition of same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions or adoption and bars LGBTI people from serving openly in the military.

Provincial mobilisation against LGBT people has state participation: the 19 December 2022 Cumhuriyet Square rally was addressed and joined by an AKP deputy mayor, and its statement framed consensual same-sex relationships as a moral collapse abroad while connecting gender and sexual rights to the government's denunciation of the Istanbul Convention.

Pride organisers nationwide have faced bans and forcible dispersal since 2015, with tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions used against marchers.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since the 29 October 2025 leak is unresolved in the sources; the inventory establishes the draft's contents and the government's stated rationale, not its final status.

Sources disagree on the reach of legal protection: the claim that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in Turkish law sits against the European Commission's 2025 assessment that protection is insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis. The scope and enforceability of the prohibition is therefore unresolved here.

The Elazığ rally evidence dates from December 2022. Whether comparable state-facilitated mobilisation is occurring in the province at present is not sourced in this inventory.

The early 2026 proposal to criminalise public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality" is described in the inventory as a measure under consideration; its legislative status is not resolved by these sources.
